title: Dusk at Green Lake
teaches: Who comes out when over a Seattle lake, high flyers and water skimmers, what they eat, and the season
summary: **Bats come out in shifts.** Big brown and silver-haired bats appear 15 to 25 minutes after sunset; the Myotis come down to the water about half an hour after sunset.
**The early bats hunt high.** Big browns and silver-haired bats hunt along and above the tree tops, with calls near 25 to 28 kHz that carry far in open air.
**The later bats skim the water.** Yuma and little brown myotis fly a metre over the lake, calling near 50 and 40 kHz.
**Smooth water helps them hunt.** It reflects their calls away like a mirror, so an insect above it gives the only echo.
**Their food comes out of the lake.** Midges, which do not bite, and caddisflies rise from the water at dusk; mosquitoes are a small share.
**A nursing mother eats close to her own weight.** For a little brown bat that is several grams a night, thousands of midges.
**The season runs April to October.** It peaks in late July and August, when pups born in June start to fly; hoary bats pass through late in summer.
**A few bats fly in winter.** Big brown and silver-haired bats sometimes wake and hunt on mild nights.

blocks.text: Green Lake fills a hollow left by the ice sheet in north Seattle, about a kilometre across, with a path round it that is busy with walkers and runners until long after dark. On a clear evening in late July the sun sets a little before nine. For the next quarter of an hour, swallows and swifts take insects over the water. Then, somewhere between 15 and 25 minutes after sunset, the first bats appear, and they do not come down to the water at all. They fly high along the tops of the trees on the far shore, fast, in long straight runs and wide turns.

Ten minutes later, as the sky goes from orange to dark blue, a second kind arrives: smaller bats that drop to within a metre of the lake and zigzag over it, so low that their reflections fly beside them. By full dark the water is busy with them. The two kinds keep apart, one in the air above the trees and one on the surface, and the second comes later. Wing shape, the pitch of their calls and the risk of being eaten explain both, as the next part shows.

The high, early bats are mostly **big brown bats** and **silver-haired bats**, weighing 8 to 20 grams against 5 to 9 for the bats that come later. They hunt in the open, along the edges of the trees and above them, and the big brown in particular is a fast flyer with wings built for open air (lesson 2). Both call near 25 to 28 kHz. A low call fades slowly in air (lesson 3), so it reaches insects 20 metres or more away, which is what a fast bat hunting in open sky needs. Big browns favour beetles and moths, big insects that give a strong echo at long range.

blocks.caption: Dusk over a Seattle lake, from 10 minutes before sunset to 70 after, in four months of the year. Pick a month and play the evening through. The hoary bat, a big, high-flying visitor described under The season below, comes only late in summer. A sketch from surveys and bat walks around Seattle lakes, not a count.

blocks.text: The water skimmers are **Myotis**, small bats of about 5 to 9 grams. Over Seattle's lakes most are **Yuma myotis**, whose calls end near 50 kHz, and **little brown myotis**, near 40 kHz. Their short, broad wings, wide for their length, turn tightly at low speed, and their short, steep calls time echoes precisely at close range, the right tools for insects a few centimetres above the surface. The surface itself helps. Smooth water reflects a call the way a mirror reflects light: sound that strikes it at a slant bounces on at the same slant, ahead and away from the bat, so very little comes back from the water, and an insect flying over it gives the only echo there is.[^mirror]

Why the Myotis come out later is less certain. The answer most researchers favour is danger. Hawks, falcons and owls hunt by sight at dusk, and a small, slow bat is easier to catch than a fast one. Across many species, fast-flying bats tend to leave their roosts earlier than slow ones, as though each waits until the light is low enough for its own escape speed.[^emerge] The insects over the water are thickest at dusk too, so a Myotis pays for its safety in lost hunting time.

parts.title: What comes out of the lake

blocks.text: Ask people what the bats over the lake are eating and most will say mosquitoes. The bats' droppings, examined under a microscope or by reading the DNA of the insects in them, say otherwise.

blocks.caption: What turns up in the droppings of three bats of Seattle's lakes, the Yuma, the little brown and the big brown, rounded from diet studies in British Columbia and Washington. Real shares change from night to night and lake to lake.
blocks.task: Guess what most of their diet is, then compare the big brown

blocks.text: For the Yuma and the little brown the answer is mostly **midges**, the small flies of the family Chironomidae. They look like mosquitoes but do not bite: the adults barely feed at all. Their larvae, red "bloodworms" in the mud on the lake bottom, can number thousands to a square metre, and on summer evenings the adults rise through the water and leave it together, the males dancing in swarms over the shore. With them come **caddisflies**, moth-like insects whose larvae build cases of sand or plant bits under water. Mosquitoes are eaten, but they are rarely common enough over open water to be more than a minor item in the droppings.

The famous figure of a thousand mosquitoes an hour goes back to experiments in a closed room in the late 1950s, where Griffin's little brown bats, flown among swarms of fruit flies or mosquitoes, caught small insects at up to about ten a minute.[^thousand] They showed how fast a bat can work, not what it eats outdoors. A wild bat eats whatever is plentiful, and over a lake at dusk that is midges.
A small bat burns its fuel fast, and a mother feeding a pup on milk burns it faster still. A nursing little brown myotis can eat close to her own body weight in insects in a night.

blocks.title: An estimate
points: A little brown bat weighs about 8 g. A nursing mother eating three quarters of that takes 6 g of insects a night.
A midge from the lake weighs about 1 to 2 mg, so 6 g is 3,000 to 6,000 midges, eaten over a few hours of hunting: one every two or three seconds.
A nursery colony of 200 mothers then takes over a kilogram of insects, roughly a million midges, in one night.

blocks.caption: How many insects a colony of little brown bats eats in a night. Pick the insect, then set the number of bats and the share of her own weight each eats in a night. Rough masses: a midge about 2 mg, a mosquito 2.5, a caddisfly 10, a moth 40.
blocks.task: Find a colony that eats a million insects in a night

blocks.text: Bats fly over Green Lake from about April to October. The numbers build through the summer: the females gather in nursery colonies in attics, bat houses and hollow trees in late spring, and each little brown or Yuma mother gives birth to a single pup in June or early July, and the pups fly at about three weeks old. Late July and August are the best evenings, with the year's young hunting beside their mothers, clumsily at first.

In late summer the **hoary bat** comes through, the heaviest bat in Washington at 20 to 35 grams, with frosted fur and long, narrow wings. It hunts high and fast over the lake and the park, and its calls near 20 kHz are low enough that some people, mostly young ones, can just hear the bottom of each call as a faint tick. Hoary bats roost alone in tree foliage and migrate south for the winter, which lesson 10 follows south, past the wind turbines that kill many of them on the way.

In winter the Myotis are in torpor, a deep, controlled chill that saves their fat (lesson 7), but big brown and silver-haired bats, which overwinter in buildings and trees around Seattle, sometimes wake on a mild night and hunt for an hour along the trees. A bat over Green Lake in January is not lost or sick; it is most likely one of these.

blocks.title: Outside
points: Pick a clear, calm evening in late July or August and look up the sunset time. Stand on the shore with open water in front and trees behind it, and start watching at sunset.
Note the minute the first bat appears high along the trees, and the minute the first one drops to the water. Do it again on another evening and compare.
Watch one water bat for a minute. Count its sudden twists and dives: each is an attempt at an insect.
A heterodyne detector (lesson L1) set near 45 kHz picks up the water bats; set near 25 kHz, the high flyers. Without one, you will hear nothing from either, except perhaps a hoary bat.

blocks.caption: Five questions on dusk at the lake
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: At a Seattle lake about 20 minutes after sunset, bats are flying fast and high along the tree tops. Which are they most likely to be?
choices: Big brown or silver-haired bats
Yuma or little brown myotis
Townsend's big-eared bats
Young bats on their first flights
items.why: The larger, faster big brown and silver-haired bats come out first and hunt high in open air. The Myotis come later and skim the water.

items.ask: Why does smooth water help a small bat find insects flying just above it?
choices: The water reflects the call away like a mirror, so the insect gives the only echo
The water amplifies every echo, so faint insects sound louder
The water is warmer than the air, so insects glow on the bat's heat sense
The water slows sound down, giving the bat more time to react
items.why: A smooth surface sends sound off at an angle, as a mirror does with light. Little comes straight back, so an insect above it stands out against near silence.

items.ask: Which best describes what Yuma and little brown myotis eat over a Seattle lake?
choices: Mostly midges and caddisflies rising from the water, with mosquitoes a small share
Mostly mosquitoes, which they seek out over still water
Mostly beetles and large moths from the trees
Mostly mayflies, the only insects that rise at dusk
items.why: Droppings show mostly non-biting midges and caddisflies, insects whose larvae live in the lake. Mosquitoes are eaten but rarely common enough over open water to matter much.

items.ask: Why are there more bats in the air over a Seattle lake in late July than in June?
choices: Pups born in June start flying and hunting
Bats arrive from eastern Washington as it gets hot
The midges hatch for the first time that year
Bats leave their winter caves only in July
items.why: Each mother has one pup in June or early July, and the pups fly at about three weeks. By late July the year's young are out with their mothers.

items.ask: A colony of 200 nursing little brown bats each eats 6 g of insects in a night. If the insects are 2 mg midges, roughly how many is that?
choices: About 600,000
About 6,000
About 60 million
About 1,200
items.why: 200 bats × 6 g is 1,200 g, or 1,200,000 mg. Divided by 2 mg a midge, that is 600,000 midges in a night.

mirror.title: An acoustic mirror
mirror.text: In the Netherlands in the 1990s, Arjan Boonman and colleagues found that Daubenton's bats, which hunt low over water as Yuma myotis do, hunted less over water covered with duckweed, which scatters echoes back. Bats take any smooth, flat surface for water: in 2010 Stefan Greif and Björn Siemers found that young bats that had never met a pond tried to drink from smooth plates of metal or plastic.

emerge.title: Light and leaving the roost
emerge.text: The idea comes from comparisons of many bat species by Gareth Jones and Jens Rydell in the 1990s: bats that fly fast and hunt in the open leave earlier in the evening than slow bats that hunt close to cover. Feeding on the dusk swarm of insects pulls the other way, and each species settles somewhere between.

thousand.title: A thousand an hour
thousand.text: Griffin and his colleagues published the room experiments in 1960. Bats gained weight fast enough while hunting to show they were catching several small insects a minute, and at peak rates of about ten a minute an hour would make six hundred. The figure grew in the retelling, and mosquitoes replaced the fruit flies.
